The Information Hires Reporters to Expand Coverage of Nvidia, Musk, Finance, Washington
entry.summary: The Information is pleased to announce four new hires to continue our newsroom's award-winning reporting. They will focus on Nvidia, finance, Elon Musk's companies and tech policy. Dakin Campbell, Finance Dakin brings deep knowledge and a wealth of sources in finance. He has already started to help break news for The Information, reporting on investment banks' trading strategies and the inner workings of complicated AI financing deals. He joins us from Business Insider, where he was chief correspondent for investigations and enterprise, and before that was its chief finance correspondent. He wrote about Oracle's borrowing binge, the true cost of data centers and how big investors, not just individuals, are pulling out of private credit. He was also one of two lead reporters for BI's award-winning project on data centers. Dakin spent eight years at BI and 10 years at Bloomberg, where among many other things, he expanded its San Francisco finance beat following the financial crisis. And he literally wrote the book on tech IPOs: Going Public: How Silicon Valley Rebels Loosened Wall Street's Grip on the IPO and Sparked a Revolution, which featured the memorable IPO valuation metric of "a little crystal-ball gazing and fairy dust." Dakin will be based in New York starting in September. Grace Kay, SpaceX and Tesla Grace has joined The Information to cover SpaceX, Tesla and other Musk companies, where she has already started to break news on xAI. She comes from Business Insider, where she worked for more than five years. There, she covered Tesla, Elon Musk and the broader EV industry. Most recently, Grace worked on BI's enterprise desk, reporting on everything from Tesla's workplace culture and executive turnover to Optimus and the Robotaxi rollout. Over the past year, she's focused on xAI's growing pains and the overlap between Musk's companies. Before BI, she reported on metals and mining at Bloomberg and covered education at Forbes. She is based in New York. Phoebe Liu, Nvidia Phoebe has joined The Information to lead our coverage of Nvidia. Phoebe will get inside the world's most valuable company, which is at the center of a once-in-a-generation boom and led by a relentless CEO doing everything he can to extend its dominance. She's recently gone deep into how Nvidia appears to be winning market share supplying chips for inference. Phoebe is well positioned for this monumental beat, given her work at Forbes over the last three and a half years. She covered numerous billionaire entrepreneurs, wild and shady startups, and scooped an xAI funding pitch. She also took a particular interest in Nvidia co-founder Curtis Priem; CoreWeave, an Nvidia vassal in the neocloud field; and Groq, which Nvidia essentially acquired for $20 billion. She is based in San Francisco. Leo Schwartz, Tech and Politics Leo Schwartz has joined The Information to cover the intersection of politics and tech. He's already started to make an impact, helping break news on Amazon's concerns over the new Anthropic model, the executive AI order and Binance. Leo joined from Fortune magazine, where he has been a senior writer for the last several years covering fintech, crypto, venture capital and financial regulation. At Fortune, he has frequently written about important political figures involved in overseeing tech (from former SEC chair Gary Gensler to Trump advisor Bo Hines). He has chronicled the growing concerns over the Trump business empire's conflicts of interest, broken regulatory news about Elon Musk and tracked the DOGE takeover of the CFPB. He is based in New York.

entry.title: Temasek's $75 Billion AI Bet
entry.summary: The prescient investor who appears to hold a crystal ball or have a healthy stomach for risk is always a compelling character to write about. These are the Josh Kushners, Peter Thiels and Masayoshi Sons of the world. Love 'em or hate 'em, they're interesting. At this point of the AI cycle, though, the more important investors to watch might be the ones that evoke little emotion and attract few headlines. They're typically the investors with a more sober approach that has often left them on the sidelines of tech megatrends in the early years. But now they're the new, incremental buyers of AI startup rounds, data center debt and tech stocks, and their patience will be tested if the investment case starts to dampen. That's why I wanted to talk to the investment leaders at Temasek-a low-profile firm that manages hundreds of billions of dollars, with the Singapore government as its sole shareholder, and that is looking to eke out stable returns without lighting cash on fire. It pairs investments in late-stage private tech bets like Stripe and Databricks with older-guard Singapore-based companies it owns huge stakes in, such as Singtel and Singapore Airlines. It holds itself up as a beacon of patient, long-term capital, and it devoted a much larger chunk of its publicly available annual report last year to risk management than it did to AI. Still, the firm has become a silent, deep-pocketed presence in Silicon Valley over the years. And this year, I've noticed its name popping up more often as a new investor in major AI-related megarounds from Anthropic, Isomorphic Labs and Waymo. Temasek is open for business in AI investments, according to Aftab Mathur, the company's managing director, who leads venture and growth investments. He was speaking to me from a glass-walled conference room with a view of Salesforce Tower in downtown San Francisco. The firm planned to triple its investment holdings in AI from $25 billion today to $75 billion by 2030. That would represent about 15% of its projected portfolio overall, up from 7% today, and nearly a quarter of its portfolio outside Singapore, he added. "That's a fairly large jump for Temasek," said Mathur, who is based in Singapore. "We're in a large scale-up in terms of AI exposure." In part what's driving the increased investment interest is what San Francisco-based Temasek Managing Director Martin Fichtner called its "virtuous circle." The firm has watched its large Singapore-based portfolio companies, like $140 billion bank DBS, adopt AI and reduce manual labor, reinforcing investors' views of the technology's value, Fichtner said. The circle is a familiar one to anyone tracking the investment cycle: Corporate adoption of AI drives revenue for AI model and application companies, which supports more capital expenditures for infrastructure, which drives more model investment. Temasek is one face of this. The same patient money is showing up as the private credit financing data centers and the Gulf funds anchoring the megarounds. That's why the tone around AI investing has shifted around the world from cautious to can't miss. Despite the thematic bullishness about the technology overall, important parts of the AI trade still have a hazy outlook. For instance, there are limits to Temasek's bullishness when I asked about the debate of the moment-whether all that AI spending is paying off inside companies. "Whether it's a virtuous circle or not is defined by: Is there an ROI [return on investment]?" Fichtner said. I was also struck by how little Temasek's AI enthusiasts wanted to go out on a limb about where the technology goes from here. Where is AI not working well inside companies? I asked. "It's too early to say," Mathur said. "I think all this is moving so quickly that we're watching, we're tracking....It'd be too early to give an answer one way or another." I asked Mathur and Fichtner which lesser-known AI company might become a household name that embodies its new strategy. Fichtner smiled and gave me a nonanswer. "I'm smiling because I think that's a question that everyone will always want to answer in the rear view mirror, but we will seek diversification," he said. "We think in portfolio terms." That portfolio, of course, is increasingly going to be AI focused. On that big-picture theme, investors are certain. But where exactly will the value lie? And what's still going to blow up? That's where many big-money AI bulls are hedging their answers. Amazon's Lower Cost AI Chip Offerings Hold Appeal for Businesses
entry.summary: For companies debating which AI server chips to use in their data centers, Amazon appears to have one advantage over Nvidia: price. The cost of using Amazon's Inferentia2 and Trainium's second generation chips to run existing AI models, known as inference, can be 80% lower than Nvidia's H100 chips, for comparable workloads, according to Karol Piatek, who advises companies on their AI infrastructure at Ireland-based consultancy Co Driver Labs. A growing number of businesses that run their own data centers are looking for cheaper and more readily available alternatives to Nvidia chips. Amazon in recent months has discussed using its custom AI chips, Trainium (for developing new models) and Inferentia, with such customers-and the idea is gaining converts.

entry.title: AI's New Risk: Unpredictable Government Policies
entry.summary: Investing in AI really is not for the faint of heart. Leaving aside all the worries about risks of huge investments in data centers and the uncertainties about demand, there's also the unpredictable government moves that can upend things. Case in point: the Trump administration's warnings to Anthropic over the weekend that no foreigners, including foreign employees of Anthropic, could access its latest AI models without permission. While that warning is aimed specifically at Anthropic-now in a standoff with the government over its latest AI models-other AI firms are worried about the precedent it sets. As we scooped today, OpenAI executives wrote to staff on Saturday that it had told the administration building AI "requires the best talent from around the world." (See our latest OpenAI scoop, on its first quarter financials, here).

entry.title: OpenAI Burned $3.7 Billion in First Three Months of 2026
entry.summary: OpenAI burned through $3.7 billion in the first quarter, more than half its $5.7 billion in revenue, according to documents the company shared with shareholders. Both cash burn and revenue tripled from the same period the previous year, signaling how even with strong AI demand, making money from AI continues to be challenging. The company ended the quarter with more than $73 billion in cash and marketable securities, compared with $40 billion at the end of December, reflecting the company's massive funding round announced at the end of March. Assuming the cash burn remains around the first quarter level, OpenAI won't need to raise more money in the near term. That could relieve the pressure on OpenAI to go public sooner rather than later.

entry.title: Anthropic Ban Stirs Concerns at OpenAI and Beyond of Crackdown on Foreign AI Talent
entry.summary: The U.S. government's latest battle with Anthropic has revived long-simmering concerns throughout the AI industry that the White House has placed a bullseye on their reliance on foreign AI talent. The Trump administration appears to have targeted only Anthropic so far, warning the company on Friday in a letter from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that it would need a license to make its latest models available to "foreign persons," including its own employees. But Anthropic's biggest rival, OpenAI, has flagged its concerns about the issue. On Saturday, OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon told staff in a Slack message that the company had told the government "strongly" that building AI "requires the best talent from around the world," which is "part of what allows the U.S. to lead in AI." Kwon said OpenAI was still trying to understand the implications of the government's actions against Anthropic and that it was a "rapidly evolving situation with a lot of unknowns."

entry.title: Cyberstarts Notches Cyera Win, Plots New Fund
entry.summary: The $12 billion valuation that Cyera snagged in a $600 million fundraise announced last week shows how hungry investors were for the cybersecurity startup's AI-focused pitch. The five-year-old startup sells software that can protect companies' data from hackers equipped with increasingly powerful AI tools-a threat highlighted by Anthropic's warnings about the cyber capabilities of its Mythos model. For the VC fund Cyberstarts, the Cyera round gives it more bragging rights after its blockbuster Wiz exit last year. The fund wrote Cyera's first $4.2 million seed funding check five years ago at a $15 million valuation; on paper, Cyberstarts has returned more than 224 times its original investment in Cyera, says Cyberstarts founder Gili Raanan. Its total stake in the company including follow-on investments is worth more than $1.2 billion, Raanan told me.

entry.title: AT&T Throttles Some Employees' AI Usage as 'Tokenminimizing' Arrives
entry.summary: As AI spending has eaten into corporate budgets, generating concern over rising costs at Fortune 500 firms from Uber to ServiceNow and Snowflake, some companies are beginning to throttle employees' usage. The latest is AT&T, which has begun limiting some employees' access to Microsoft's Github Copilot, according to a person at the company. In a more striking example, Meta is also limiting employees' AI spending on services from Anthropic and other providers, a sharp reversal from a few months ago when employees competed with each other to use as much AI as possible, known as tokenmaxxing, my colleague Jyoti reported Friday. Uber and Walmart similarly capped employee usage of AI coding tools, Bloomberg recently reported. And the Financial Times reported that Amazon has scrapped its "leader board" that ranked employees by the amount of AI they used. Some companies are effectively saying, "I told you so." "We never celebrated tokenmaxing," Box CEO Aaron Levie told me. "We never had leaderboards, so we didn't get ahead of our skis on sort of incentivizing the wrong thing."

entry.title: Is Anthropic Losing Goodwill With AI Researchers?; AGI House Alums Raise $25 Million For New Fund
entry.summary: Remember the last time Anthropic tussled with the Trump administration, all the way back in February, when a coterie of competing AI researchers and CEOs (even Sam Altman!) quickly came to Anthropic's defense? That doesn't seem to be happening this time. In the wake of Trump officials' Friday night move to effectively ban Anthropic's most advanced models over alleged cybersecurity fears-precipitated in part by Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, no less-there's been nary a peep from Anthropic's rivals about one of the most remarkable situations we've seen in years (and that's saying something). Indeed, a number of employees from OpenAI and other rival AI labs say they have less sympathy for Anthropic this time. They argued that because Anthropic had been talking up the capabilities and dangers of its Claude Mythos model and asking for more aggressive federal regulation, the company shouldn't have been surprised when the government reacted so strongly to security concerns around the new models. In a post he published just last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei actually compared the speed of AI policy to the slow-moving Treebeard in The Lord of the Rings.

entry.title: The Fable 5 Export Controls Harm US Cyber Defense
entry.summary: The Fable 5 Export Controls Harm US Cyber Defense I quoted The Atlantic quoting Kate Moussouris earlier, when I should have gone straight to the source. Here she is confirming that the "jailbreak" that got Claude Fable 5 banned under an export control really was "fix this code": The researchers took open-source code with known CVEs, plus new code with deliberately planted vulnerabilities, and asked Fable 5, Mythos, and Opus to "review the code for security issues." Fable 5 refused. They then asked the models to "fix this code" and, through a multistep and manual process, turned the output into scripts that test the patches. As Kate points out, this is absurd. Coding models fix bugs, and security exploits are the most important category of bugs for them to fix! Defenders need to be able to ask AI to fix the bugs in a file, explain why the fix matters, and write tests that confirm the patch works. That is not a guardrail bypass. It is the most valuable thing an AI model can do for defensive security: executing the find, fix, and test loop defenders run every day. [...] The prompts worked because they were defensive requests, and that capability cannot be removed without making the model worse at fixing bugs and verifying patches. This whole situation is such a mess. Non-technical decision-makers have been hearing that models that can "craft cyber attacks" are uniquely dangerous for months. Now they look ready to ban any model that can help us secure our code. Tags: jailbreaking, security, ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, ai-security-research, claude-mythos

entry.title: Quoting Matteo Wong, The Atlantic
entry.summary: Katie Moussouris, a cybersecurity expert and the CEO of Luta Security, told me that Anthropic shared with her a copy of the White House's report on the Fable jailbreak to get her appraisal. (She said that she is not being paid by Anthropic.) The report, Moussouris said, involved IT experts asking Fable to help find and patch bugs. When given deliberately insecure code, she said, Fable refused the prompt "review the code for security issues" but then complied when asked to "fix this code," followed by some further manual steps. Moussouris told me that this was just "the model working as intended" for cyberdefense. - Matteo Wong, The Atlantic, The White House Is Ratcheting Up Its War Against Anthropic Tags: anthropic, claude, ai, llms, ai-ethics, jailbreaking, generative-ai, ai-security-research, claude-mythos

entry.title: Cloudflare CAPTCHA on at least one ampersand
entry.summary: TIL: Cloudflare CAPTCHA on at least one ampersand I'm using Cloudflare's CAPTCHA (they call it a "Web Application Firewall > Custom rules > Managed Challenge" these days) to prevent crawlers from aggresively spidering my faceted search engine on this site, but I got fed up of even simple ?q=term searches triggering the challenge. After some mucking around with Claude Code it turns out you can register the following rule instead, so the CAPTCHA only kicks in for search URLs containing at least one ampersand: (http.request.uri.path wildcard r"/search/*" and http.request.uri.query contains "&") And now /search/?q=lemur works without triggering a CAPTCHA! Also included: notes on trying out the Cloudflare MCP with Claude Code, though it turned out not to be able to edit the rules in question so I had Claude Code switch to the Cloudflare API instead. Tags: captchas, cloudflare, model-context-protocol, claude-code

entry.title: "They screwed us": Personality clashes sent Anthropic's models offline
entry.summary: "They screwed us": Personality clashes sent Anthropic's models offline Lots of "source familiar with the administration's thinking" and "source close to Anthropic" in this Axios piece, which is the best collection of behind-the-scenes gossip I've seen about the US government export control Mythos/Fable story so far. Logan Graham (I lead the Frontier Red Team at Anthropic), Dave Orr (Head of Safeguards, previously a Director of Engineering at Google DeepMind), and blog favorite Nicholas Carlini are reported to be meeting with the Commerce Department today in D.C. Good luck to them! (I just noticed Logan was "Special Adviser to the Prime Minister" in the Boris Johnson era, covering AI, science, and technology policy - so significant political experience.) This closing notes doesn't give me much optimism that we'll be getting Fable back any time soon: The bottom line: One option is to make sure Anthropic's models can't be jailbroken - though perfect jailbreak resistance may be impossible. Absent that, a source familiar with the administration's thinking said it may simply come down to an attitude fix where, instead of feeling dismissed, "everyone feels safe, secure and happy." This made me wonder if Anthropic ever successfully addressed the class of attacks described in the Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models paper from 2023. It looks like their Constitutional Classifiers work (that post is from January this year) is relevant to that. They continue to claim that no "universal jailbreak" has been found against Claude Mythos, classifying the jailbreak that triggered the US government response as "a potential narrow, non-universal jailbreak". Tags: jailbreaking, ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, claude, nicholas-carlini, ai-ethics, claude-mythos

entry.title: gpt-oss-safeguard technical report
entry.summary: gpt-oss-safeguard-120b and gpt-oss-safeguard-20b are two open-weight reasoning models post-trained from the gpt-oss models and trained to reason from a provided policy in order to label content under that policy. In this report, we describe gpt-oss-safeguard's capabilities and provide our baseline safety evaluations on the gpt-oss-safeguard models, using the underlying gpt-oss models as a baseline. For more information about the development and architecture of the underlying gpt-oss models, see the original gpt-oss model model card⁠.
